utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Sarah Clanton, Case Manager Thomas Laugel, legal intern Marina Marcikic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hadzic, I remind you that you are still under oath. Mr. Stringer, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: To start with this morning, I'd like to go back to an exhibit we looked momentarily yesterday, which is Exhibit 1D03600, and the tab number for that I failed to note.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is the newspaper article we looked at yesterday, and you weren't able to find the relevant part of the text that I was wanting to discuss with you in the original language version, and I think it turns out that actually if we just go to the next page of the B/C/S version, we will find what we're looking for. That's it. So that was my mistake. I just forgot to take you to the next page. So this -- and, again, we're still on the subject of Mr. Stevo Bogic. This is from the 16th of July, 1991, the Danas publication. And does it now appear to you, Mr. Hadzic, that the B/C/S text that you can read corresponds to the English translation, if you're able to say that. This is an article entitled: "No talks with the Croats." And then it starts off: "In Borovo Selo, since the clashes in May, no journalists from the north-west have been in Borovo Selo ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And in that first paragraph there, there are some words attributed to Mr. Bogic, and he says there that Croatian authorities had issued several wanted notices against him, and they were just waiting for Serbia to recognise as its own territory Slavonia, Baranja, and Srem. He goes on to say that: "Too many insults, too many victims fell, so living together is no longer possible." This being in July, Mr. Hadzic, I understand from your earlier testimony that during this period you were actually spending time living in Borovo when you were unable to get to your home town of Pacetin because of the roads. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, you didn't understand that quite right. I did not live in Borovo at the time. I didn't have anyone to stay with. I was in Borovo Selo sometimes once a week or once every two weeks, I spent two or three hours there. I didn't live there at the time. That's not where I slept. I was with my family in a village near Sombor, and all of a sudden, I simply cannot remember the name of that village where we were staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And on the transcript from July 8th, on page 9534 to 9535, your counsel asked you -- first of all, he is asking you: "Where did you spend your time. Did you live in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem all the time or did you live in Serbia, like in May 1991?" You said, this was your answer: "My family were refugees in Serbia and I usually return in the evenings and spent the night with them. During the day I spent most of my time in Borovo Selo. And if I was able to find a car, sometimes I would go to Pacetin." So maybe my question wasn't the best one. So the question now would be: During, say, this period of May, were you spending a good portion of the day in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I came to Borovo Selo only in the second half of the first half of May. That would be after the 10th of May. And then on the 15th of May, again I tried. That's when Vula drowned. What I said has to do with the second part or the end of May. That is to say that I would spend the day there, but I would not spend the night there. I mean, your question, the one that has do with this text, I thought that that related to July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right. We're going to get there. And actually we'll go there with my next question because again referring back to your direct examination, Mr. Zivanovic asked you if you remembered journalists and reporters making a visit to Borovo, both foreign and domestic press, in those days of July 1991. And your answer was yes, you did remember that, and that you sometimes had occasion to meet with them. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, and that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then actually what followed, then, was you were asked to comment on a different newspaper article which is now already in evidence, which is D118, which was the 13th of July article in the Politika. And so I would just want to ask you now about this other exhibit that we see, 3600, which is three days later now on the 16th of July, 1991. So does this article also refer to that period you just were -- had described earlier about when you had an opportunity to speak to journalists who had come to Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this article that's on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's right. We can go down to the second paragraph and you'll see that there are some statements there that are attributed to you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to see that first in order to be able to answer your question. I just need a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's the paragraph that begins with the words: "Instead of having a national council, Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem have, since recently, had their own government."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, but none of the paragraphs in B/C/S begins with these words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, in the article, do you see a quote -- well, do you see a reference to what I've just described even if the words aren't exact. A reference to instead of having a national council, SBWS now has a government, Hadzic as its president, says that its first task is for these areas to be joint to Serbia as soon as possible. And then it goes on to refer to Mr. Devetak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, if this question could be put after the -- Mr. Hadzic read complete article. He was asking the time to read this -- this article from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's right. I apologise, I was simply trying to direct Mr. Hadzic to the part that I'm interested in, but if he wants to take more time to read it, that's fine. I see that it's in Latin script. It would be the second paragraph of the original language version. I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I see it and I've read it just now. I did not give that statement. I see that these are Croatian journalists. I did not give any statements for the Croatian press at that time. And he's not quoting me. This journalist is giving his own comment. But if I understand this properly, he talked to Vitomir Devetak and Stevo Bogic, not me, and I'm not even sure that he talked to them. That's the way it looks on the basis of what has been written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we have the next page in English, please. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's do this, Mr. Hadzic. I don't want to spend too much time on this. But let's look at the words of Mr. Devetak here. In that paragraph it says: "Vitomir Devetak, who held a press conference in a domestic and foreign journalists in an abandoned school hall, believes that Serbia is hesitant." And then it goes on. He refers to: "56 villages from Slavonia, Baranja, with a Serbian population are tied to Borovo." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have D118, which is the article from the 13th of July that came into evidence during Mr. Hadzic's direct examination. I don't have a tab number for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this is an article that you looked at on your direct exam, Mr. Hadzic, and that you then -- that was then put into evidence. I'd like to direct your attention under the -- first of all, if we could blow it up. This is the article called: "A place of men, impressions of foreign journalists." And the second section of it is under the heading: "Peaceful separation." And I know it's small text. If we could find a way to blow that up. I can also give you my hard copy, if you'd like, although it's small text.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember you gave it to me last time as well. And, again, the print was very fine, and I couldn't see. Could they just blow up that part of the text? A bit more, to the right. Now they should scroll down. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The article begins: "Borovo Selo, July. The cease-fire, the hardest one, which is only apparent, has lasted for a few days ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't read any of this that is written here. Actually, I can read half of it, and I cannot read the other half.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Why are you unable to read the other half? I don't recall you had any difficulty reading this when it was shown to you on direct examination, sir. That's when I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said I can read half of it, I don't mean exact halves. I can read one letter and then I cannot read another one, so in a sentence, I can read, say, half a word.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll just make a large copy of it, and we'll come back to this a third time and see if we can make it work, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, could we please have tab 1420, and this is an under-seal document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Tab 1420. It is P1382.1351. It's under seal. So perhaps we should go into private session. Although, if we don't broadcast it, Mr. President, perhaps -- well, I think to be safe, if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is minutes of the District Council of the SBWS meeting held in Erdut on 6th of July, 1992. And here we see present are members of the District Council. This is Milan Ilic. We've talked about him. Pajo Nedic. I asked you about him yesterday. Other members of the district council. And then other people present, Jovo Rebraca. Who is he, Mr. Jovo Rebraca?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rebraca was president of Tenja municipality at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Djordje Calosevic, who was he?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was president of Dalj municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was he also a member or did he hold a leadership position in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not a leader. I believe he was a member of the SDS. But, at that time, there was a moratorium on the work of political parties. The SDS was not active.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then then moving down, we see that Stevo Bogic now is attending this meeting. Do you know whether it was -- whether as part of his duties as deputy prime minister, Mr. Bogic would have been attending meetings like this, things happening at the more local level as opposed to the federal level or the republican level?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was his duty. I don't think so under the constitution. You asked me yesterday what his title was but I saw it now. You saw he was at that meeting with Vejzovic. He co-ordinated the work and helped the prime minister, so that's how we can see what his job was. But at that time I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So that here he would be acting as a representative of the prime minister at this district council meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just guessing. I really know nothing about that session. I didn't know when it was being held. I'm seeing this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you have a personal or friendship relationship with Mr. Djordje Calosevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. I knew him, but I did not have any particular relationship?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you -- did he ever accompany you to meetings or to social functions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never went to meetings together with me, but he did attend some meetings. Not really accompanying me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What about social functions, either during this period or later?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. There were a lot of developments and events, but I don't remember whether Calosevic was there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tender 65 ter 6532, the minutes of this District Council meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object because the witness doesn't know anything about this meeting and this document -- particular document and there is no foundation for admitting this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, can you go to the last page of the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could go to the last page of the original language version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Whether you recognise the stamp and/or the signature?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this stamp for the first time. It must be the new stamp of the District Council. Yesterday you asked me about Milan Ilic's signature. I saw it for the first time yesterday, but this is completely different. It's not the same thing as the one yesterday. I don't know who signed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, this is Mr. Jovan Jovicic, I believe. That's what the translation indicates.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the technical staff. I never heard that name. I never heard that he occupied any position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "technical staff"? Like, was he a secretary or an administrator?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that this is really "Jovan Jovicic" written here. Jovan Jovicic did not exist in an important position. I think he was an unimportant person. I don't know exactly what the name is, Jovan Jovicic or Jovic. I don't know whose signature this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, we don't disagree, do we, that during this period of time Mr. Milan Ilic was the president of the District Council for SBWS; is that correct? We can agree on that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said that at least ten times. From spring 1992 he was elected the -- the elected president of that District Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just on that, as the president of the District Council did he sort of -- was he the leading executive, the leader of the executive body for SBWS then?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by the very name of that title, that's what it means. But I didn't meddle in their work, and I don't know to what extent they made any decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I've just been informed that I misspoke, I said "Jovan" and I should have said "Nemanja," I think, which is the name as it appears on the translation. Nemanja Jovcic. Do you know who that is, Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that he was at the meeting. I personally didn't know him. Now I see that it's not Jovicic by Jovcic, first name Nemanja. I don't know what his position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 63, 1D03460. This may be a confidential document, Mr. President. If we could not broadcast, I think I can work with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, the first part of this document, the first page, and by the way, just for the record, this is dated -- we're jumping ahead in time now to the 24th of May, 1994. And this is a report of some -- of an event that took place on the 21st of May and it refers to Mr. Seselj attending a meeting of SRS, Serbian Radical Party representatives in Borovo Naselje. I actually am going to skip over that part because it's not what is of interest here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 of the English version. In the B/C/S version, it's the last paragraph of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it refers to the village feast day in Pacetin. At this time, you're the former president of the RSK. You had organised a party. Take a look at that, Mr. Hadzic, and tell us if you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that celebration of the patron saint's day specifically. There were many people there. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It is indicated here that Mr. Bogic attended this event as well as Mr. Djordje Calosevic, Boro Bogunovic. The party was festive, there was a band. And also there's a reference to Mr. Misa Milosevic who was present. And on him, Mr. Misa Milosevic, his name has come up before in connection with your participation in the international negotiations, correct? He accompanied you and Mr. Babic, I believe, in some of the early negotiations with Mr. Wijnaendts and the Carrington Commission. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true we mentioned Misa Milosevic. At that time when we mentioned him, that was the autumn of 1991, I didn't know him. He was in a delegation of the SAO Krajina headed by Milan Babic. That's when I first heard of him, and I met him a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you remember him attending a party that you hosted in your village, the event that's referred to here? Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. Misa was in Pacetin only once, together with Momo Kapor. But, for instance, a person, Djuro Kljajic is mentioned here. I don't know such a person so he couldn't ever have been in my house. Nobody with that name has ever visited me. But I cannot say about these names that they were either there or not because there were over 50 people there, coming and going.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogic has been a guest in your house, I take it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Pacetin very rarely. I don't remember that he was ever in Pacetin. But I should like to tell the Trial Chamber, in the Serbian Orthodox religion, you don't invite people to your patron saint's day. People who know who are your friends will come on their own. There were some people who came from Belgrade, from a long way away, and the rest were locals. But none of them were specifically invited. You don't invite people, that's our custom. You don't invite people on that day. They come on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Djordje Calosevic, he has also been a guest in your house, whether on this occasion or other occasions; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlier when I was the president of the republic, he didn't come. And later, when I lost the elections, I don't know why he would come then. Maybe he had come earlier to congratulate me, to express his support. But I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1014. This is a video-clip. And it is 65 ter 4811.4, and we'll wait for the interpreters to let us know when they've found it. While we're waiting for the interpreters, Mr. President, I have just been informed by my colleague Ms. Clanton that the document we just looked at a moment ago, 1D03460, is a public exhibit from the Stanisic-Simatovic case, and so it may not be necessary to have confidential status linked to this document for our case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we can lift that status.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Dafina Milanovic with her associates visited Baranja and Srem today. Stevo Bogic, deputy prime minister of the Republic of Serbian Krajina; Milan Ilic, president of the District Council of the Serbian District; Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, commander of the Serbian Volunteer Guard; and a group of businessmen from the district welcomed her in Erdut. During her meeting, Mrs. Milanovic inquired about the economic situation and possibilities to invest in the revival of economy. She said that the possibilities and potential of the district are huge and the potential of Krajina has to be used in a proper way for the benefit of the people, Serbian Krajina, and its future. "Dafina Milanovic: I believe we could make it become better than Switzerland. Having in mind the potential of Krajina, it would be easy to achieve if we start to work more and if we show more responsibility. The situation will get better once we start employing people. It is my intention first to build a greenhouse, to start producing food because that's what is most needed in Serbian Krajina. Then we would start with livestock farming. I talked yesterday with businessmen from Thessaloniki and Athens about investments in the livestock export industry here as well, as well as a dairy plant, and I think we will start working on it very soon. "Another speaker: If Mrs. Dafina is of the opinion that our area could become ... we have no reason to doubt it. It is our duty to work on it and make it happen."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, we'll take another look at the video, Mr. Hadzic, but just the very last person who was speaking, can you tell us who that was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's start the video again and we'll stop at a couple of places. I'm going to ask you to identify some more people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, and before we go further, Mr. Hadzic, I should ask, can you tell us who is this woman, Dafina Milanovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She had a privately owned bank, as far as I remember, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And can you identify the two men who are then on either side of her, holding the flag, in the image that we're just looking at here.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the right of her, as you all well know, is Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and to her left, I can identify Milan Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What period of time was Mr. Ilic - if you know - the president of the SBWS District Council?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I know it was from spring 1992 until -- I'm not sure when.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Why did he wear a uniform if is he a civilian, holding down a civilian position as president of the District Council?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can ask me -- you're asking me too much as a witness. From my information, I never heard why he was wearing a uniform. Milan Ilic is dead, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: At the beginning of your cross-examination before the summer recess when we were talking about Arkan I showed you an exhibit which was P1909, in which a reference was made to Ilic being fond of wearing the Tigrovi uniform. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember you said that, but that was the first time I heard about it. I didn't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, what we see here is -- from what we can see, it appears he is wearing something very similar to the Arkan that -- to the uniform that Arkan is wearing, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could just roll the video for a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. Hadzic, who are we looking at here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevo Bogic. In the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in the footage, he's introduced as deputy prime minister of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, so this would at least be sometime in or after the spring of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992/1993. I really don't know exactly when it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tender this clip, 65 ter 4811.4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3224, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1720. 65 ter 6562. It's a confidential document, which I think -- if we don't broadcast it on the screens outside, I can manage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is a report, Mr. Hadzic, dated 13th of October, 1993. It's coming from Belgrade. It's referring to a session of the Assembly of the SBWS that was held in Dalj on the 11th of October. And then another session that was held the following day, on the 12th of October, in Vukovar. And at that session, Deputy Stevo Bogic and Boro Bogunovic forced and pressured deputies who wanted to go to the continuation of the session at Plitvice, saying they would not get there. Take a look, take a moment to look at the document, Mr. Hadzic, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would kindly ask that this document Mr. Hadzic could read in its entirety because it is just recently disclosed, and I don't believe that he had the opportunity earlier to see that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can give him my hard copy, Mr. President, if that would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think that would. Thank you, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're asking me about this document, I think it's a pamphlet infiltrated at the beginning of the election campaign in the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It -- what is -- what I'm not interested in is the -- if there is sort of some political competition that is taking place between you and Mr. Martic, his people and your people, we're not interested in that. We see that this is in the leadup to the election that occurred in December of 1993. The question I have, though, is at the bottom of the last paragraph on the first page of the English version, which begins with the words: "In the process, the citizens do not believe all these statements because they know ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the second page in Serbian. Now I see it. I have it in my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And actually in the preceding paragraph there's a reference here in this report to a statement that's attributed to you that: "Slobodan Milosevic has been informed of everything, that Hadzic is in daily contact with him, along the lines of: I agreed on this too with Slobo a moment ago." And then it goes on to say: "In the process, citizens do not believe all these statements because they know that actually in question is an attempt of a group of criminals, headed by President Hadzic, Steve Bogic, Boro Bogunovic, Vukasin Egic, Jovan Rebraca and others, to retain a monopoly over the material goods of the [sic] region." And then it continues on. We can all read that.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's important also to read that the Socialist Party of Serbia is also mentioned. That says it all about this text. And it shows the purpose of this text. The target audience.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, in the video-clip that we just saw where Mr. Bogic, Arkan and Ilic and all the businessmen were meeting with Ms. Milanovic, there was an objective of acquiring control over the material wealth of that region, the SBWS, and people who'd been with you from the beginning, such as Stevo Bogic and Arkan, were a big part of that. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm a bit stunned by your logic and linking this document to what we were discussing and the visit of Dafina Milanovic in Erdut. First of all, I think that has nothing to do with it. And secondly, during the war, in the former Croatia, there was a lot of crime on both sides, the Croatian side and the Serb side. And there's no denying that. Dafina Milanovic came only once. I don't know anything about that. And now whether Arkan was involved in crime or somebody else, I really don't know. The judiciary hasn't said anything about it so I can only make assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1037.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We're going to change gears here, Mr. Hadzic, take on a new topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is a video-clip. 65 ter 4873.2. And we'll wait for the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Anchor: As previously announced, Goran Hadzic, president of the Serb region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem is in our studio. Good evening. "Goran Hadzic: Good evening. "Anchor: When did you arrive in Belgrade? "Goran Hadzic: Well, I arrived last night. "Anchor: Can I ask you as a reporter what the current situation in the war theatre is? "Goran Hadzic: Well, the situation is much clearer in military terms. We have a big part of free liberated territory in our area. That is, the whole of Baranja, Western Srem, from Vinkovci in the direction of Sid, and the bigger part of this Osijek field. That is, the territory between Osijek and Vukovar. Vukovar is currently blocked. We expect a denouement of the situation in Vukovar any day. We are capable of dealing with this quickly, but we are thinking of human lives and taking care that this would be done slowly and securely with as little casualties as possible. That is, we do not want any casualties."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Hadzic, based on your description of the situation here, Vukovar is still blocked, this would indicate to us that we're talking about the period obviously prior to the 18th of November, 1991, sometime perhaps in earlier November, October 1991 [Realtime transcript read in error "1992"]. Is that generally the time-frame here, based on what you've said?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it could be that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the information that you're sharing with the reporter here, who was briefing you on the military situation, status, operations objective, what was the source of your information that you're giving us here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already explained this to you maybe once. I gave information on the basis of the knowledge I had as an ordinary citizen and from the media and -- I had the opportunity of buying newspapers in Serbia. In Slavonia and Baranja, people could not read the newspapers or see the electronic media. Also I got information from friends, some ministers at meetings, et cetera. It was unofficial but I didn't want to say on TV that I did not know because in this way, I would do away with my political position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You just said you "had the opportunity of buying newspapers in Serbia. In Slavonia or Baranja, people could not read the newspapers or see the electronic media." So are you telling us that all of the information you got about what was happening was coming to you from the newspapers in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether this interpretation is good, what I said just now. I think that you've misquoted me just now. Perhaps it's a mistake in the transcript, so I'm going to repeat what I said. I said that in Slavonia and Baranja there weren't any newspapers and there wasn't any television. People couldn't watch television because there usually wasn't electricity. And I bought newspapers in Serbia. When I was in Serbia, I could see the Belgrade media and the Zagreb media and I even found a way of obtaining Croatian newspapers, too, so I got information from both sides, the Serb and the Croat sides. Because I had to be very careful about this. I didn't have a particular service, a police or military police that would inform me, so that was the only way in which I received information, the way I described just now, through Croatian and Serbian media and a bit through foreign media. But my English was not at that level that I could understand 100 per cent of everything, so it was mostly the Serbian media and the Croatian media.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you read in the Serbian media or in the media that denouement on the situation in Vukovar could come any day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I notice that one word was omitted from the transcript. In -- at page 25, line 8, after the word "a police or military" -- the word "military" was omitted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said that I did not have that kind of service. I did not have a police or a military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stringer. It's on the record now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Also I think either I misspoke or there was a mistake on page 24, line 6, I was suggesting to Mr. Hadzic that this was sometime prior to 18th of November, 1991, and then I said sometime perhaps in earlier November or October 1992, and that obviously actually should be 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer. It's on the record now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you were going to Belgrade frequently. We know that during the fall of 1991 you were meeting with people in the Ministry of Defence. We're going to talk about your meeting with Mr. Mandaric in a little while in Novi Sad. The fact is, you were getting your information not from the press but from military and political people whom you were meeting throughout this period of time. Why don't you just admit that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I admit that when that is not true? I'm not being forced to say something in terms of admitting or not admitting. I'm testifying here. I'm not here to admit this or that. I'm testifying about what things were like. As for the people you mentioned, they actually asked me about what was going on there, specifically Mandaric and the Defence Ministry, and they didn't know anything what was going on over there. They knew even less than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So when you are saying things like: "We expect denouement of the situation in Vukovar any day, we are capable of dealing with this quickly, we are thinking of human lives," this is all just stuff you are making up? I mean, you wouldn't be reading about that in the press, I don't think. Is this just a political statement you're making?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could interpret it any which way you want but that was my conclusion. This was my sublimation of this situation and that is what I wanted to say in public, so you can say that I made it up or that I provided information halfway or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We're continuing with the video but I'm not hearing any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear anything.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We just heard half a second of the soundtrack now, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Anchor: Do you have information on events in Vukovar? Do you have information on Serb people in Zagreb? All communication lines are down, there is no phone connection, people cannot talk to their families. "Goran Hadzic: As I said, I'm not concerned with military issues. I am positive a final solution will follow. I'm, however, concerned about the information I personally received from some of our services. They tell me what the situation in Zagreb is, and we know what happened in Vukovar, mass crime against the civilian population. We will interrogate perpetrators and bring them to court, national court. I am certain they will be published [as interpreted] accordingly for their misdeeds. It is no use to whine. This is neither asked nor expected of us. Serbs never whined. Serbs should fight and will fight to protect their people. "Anchor: You have already appealed to all able-bodied men to return to their homes and join their comrades who are already at the frontline. Was the appeal successful? "Goran Hadzic: The appeal was successful in every way. A number of our combatants who fled now returned. They are fighting in the first lines. We also called volunteers from Serbia, irrespective of their party, Serbs to join our ranks and fight with Serb insignia for the imperilled Serb people. They came. I will take this opportunity to thank all of them who came to fight. The group from Belgrade stands out. They are always in the first combat lines. They fight and get killed just like us but are not hesitant to go all the way and win. "Anchor: What do you think, those of you who are in the field, what is the actual condition that could lead to a truce, not the one signed in cabinets but the actual truce in theatre of war? "Goran Hadzic: Well, there is a number of conditions. The first one is for Serbs to come to their senses - I refer to all Serbs within the current borders of Yugoslavia - and realise that only Serb unity can lead to final victory. The second condition is that official Europe, that is the world, the international community, realise that the Yugoslav problem can only be realised by respecting the will of the people, in no other way. No foreign interference can help with this. And the third condition is to deal with this Fascist Ustasha nest in the Republic of Croatia till the end firmly and decisively. This means confronting them with no mercy since they inflicted so much evil on the suffering Serb people that there is no mercy for them, nor should there be. "Anchor: Do you think that Serbs and Croats can live together? "Goran Hadzic: Not the brotherhood and unity type of co-existence introduced 50 years ago, but knowing my people, I'm sure Serb will not harm anyone who is not harming them. So all Croats who stay in our region, all Croats living here for years, like us, will be able to stay with us in the Serb region, have the same rights as everyone else, as Serb people, other nations and nationalities. And the Croats who have blood on their hands and are wallowing in it, they will surely be held responsible for what they did. We will have no mercy with them, and U say this for the third time this evening. "Anchor: Thank you for being the guest of Dnevnikov Dodatak. We are moving on now."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hadzic, this testimony you've been giving us about having as your only sources what you read in the newspaper in Belgrade, you've just lied about that because now as you've said publicly and at the time, you were getting information from what you referred to as "our services." Who are "our services" that you referred to in this televised interview?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not a lawyer and I have to give a sincere answer to this question. If I were to say now that I had some service that provided information to me, I think that it would be the duty of all in this courtroom, the Prosecutors and the Judges, they would say: Yes, which services? Why are you lying? I wanted to sound important, to attach some importance to myself. It's a silly lie. When I say everyone knows -- well, of course, this is the first time you hear it, but I say everyone in Slavonia and Baranja knows, what kind of service? I had no service. I heard about the suffering of Serbs in Zagreb through the Serb media and some personal information from individuals, refugees who returned. As for the suffering of Serbs in Vukovar, I heard about that from the Serbs who had fled from Vukovar so ... so these were these services of mine. My services. If I were to say now that I had some service, I would be lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just like you were lying then, as you say, when you gave this interview?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm under oath here. And it doesn't really suit me to say anything that is false or to lie. But, at that time, I was a politician. I was making statements. You can call that a lie, but I just exaggerated things. I wanted to point out how important this information I had was. That was my intention. It wasn't my intention to lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hadzic, you lie when it suits you. Just as you're lying here today because you think it suits you to lie here today and to minimise the level of your involvement and knowledge of what was going on. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that's not true. If I said some information that was wrong or exaggerated things a bit, that doesn't mean that that was my intention. When somebody says that I destroyed mosques, I didn't say that they were lying although it's obvious [Realtime transcript read in error "often"] that that was not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It also suited you in your role as prime minister of the SBWS during this period to stoke hatred and to encourage violence with the words that you're issuing here, no mercy, three times, as you said, and already you're setting the stage for the events that occurred once Vukovar fell and the prisoners were taken off to Ovcara, that is, the punishment for misdeeds. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I notice in the last answer of Mr. Hadzic in -- it is page 30, line 15, the word "often." As far as I know he didn't mention this word at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Should we ask Mr. Hadzic to repeat his answer, Mr. Zivanovic? Because I'm not quite sure I can make anything of it with the word "often" or without the word "often."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he could repeat. Maybe we can read out whole -- whole answer between lines 12 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll read the answer. Mr. Hadzic, you gave to Mr. Stringer's question: "Of course, that is not true. If" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course -- he didn't use the word "often."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment. This is on the record: "Of course, that is not true. If I" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: "If I said some information that was wrong or exaggerated things a bit, that doesn't mean that that was my intention. When somebody says that I destroyed mosques, I didn't say that they were lying although it's often that that was not true."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, "often" is there unnecessarily. I mean, I'm not impolite and I'm not saying that they lied. I am just saying that it's not true. So it's a mistake. Very often this makes no sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So your answer is: I do not -- I'm not saying that they were lying although it is not true. That's your answer, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Not to get too technical but could I inquire whether the Registrar, whether these sorts of interventions and clarifications are held against the Prosecution for its time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Registrar says yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It seems unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry about that, Mr. Stringer. A little misunderstanding. The answer is no, it is not on your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I want to just move quickly here in the next few minutes before the break, Mr. Hadzic. Continuing in the video, we can go back if you'd like but you were asked about an appeal that you had made to all able-bodied men to return their homes, join their comrades who were already in the front. You were asked if the appeal was successful and you said the appeal was successful in every way. So just to clarify, I think I'm going to suggest to you that you're referring there to the mobilisation order that you issued on the 23rd of August, 1991. We looked at once before. We could look at it again if you want. It's P3217. But could we agree there that you're referring to the mobilisation order that you'd issued?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's possible, but you put a question to me and then my lawyer intervened and then I didn't answer that question. And, in my view, the conclusion that you drew is very wrong and I am really bothered by that, and I cannot leave from here without explaining that. You said that I stoked hatred and that I called for revenge and that is totally contrary to what I had intended. I don't know whether there's enough time for me to explain this before the break or should I do it after the break because that's the question that you put and then you moved on to a different question and then I didn't answer to -- answer this. So if Their Honours remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Perhaps it's best left for after the break because I'm sure there will be some follow-up on that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we take the first break. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I want to stay on the issue of the volunteers. We just saw the videotape where you were on the news broadcast in Belgrade. Actually, no. Before the break, we were going to continue with this issue of your words that we just saw, the issue of what I called stoking up the public. Here, in the video - three times as you said - saying that there would be no mercy to those involved in, with blood on their hands, as you said, I believe, those wallowing in the blood. So you wanted to tell the Chamber what you meant when you were talking like that. So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to say that my intention was completely the opposite of what the Prosecutor called stoking up. I'll be very brief. I had relatively very little political experience. I had only been active in my own village as the class president, et cetera. But I realised from primary school that whenever somebody has a contrary opinion, in order to get through to that person and to prove that he is not right, I have to apparently agree at first in order to achieve my aim and that is to persuade that person. So, in the beginning, I always made a semblance of agreeing with that person but, at the end, I would say that the criminals will be tried in the end and their guilt proven. I didn't -- that's why I said, at first, that the criminals will be dealt with without trial. I'm sorry if somebody misunderstood this here, but I'm telling you what my intention was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just like before the recess, you indicated that you were sorry if people who heard you talking about ancestors of the Western Herzegovinians who had moved up into the SBWS region, you were sorry if people interpreted your words about them to be some sort of an incitement. So this is just another example that, as you say, you didn't really mean what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You abused my explanation, which was a general explanation. This matter is completely different. I said I was sorry for the people who hailed from Western Herzegovina and who were not Ustashas. Although we know that from that region there were many people who were Ustashas. We know very well who Ustashas were, who Hitler was, who were Fascists. It's a completely different example. It has nothing to do with what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, despite the fact that your only experience in politics, apparently, was being the class president, you knew full well the effect that words like this would have on the listening public. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, but I didn't see any reference in the last document or the video presented here about people from -- from Western Herzegovina. He spoke about Croats but not particularly about the people from Western Herzegovina. If I could see the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll provide a reference, Mr. President. I don't have it handy. My recollection is that we spoke extensively with Mr. Hadzic about a series of public statements he had made condemning people, families, ancestors of those who had moved into the region from Western Herzegovina during the Ante Pavelic time in 1941. That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was some interview published in -- on 4th September 1991. But in this particular document, he never put any difference between Croats and -- Croats from Western Herzegovina. In this video. I -- I didn't -- I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Are you sure [Microphone not activated]?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this particular video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, without using the word "Herzegovina Croats" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Western -- Croats from Western Herzegovina in this particular document. I didn't see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- didn't use that word in this video. But unless I'm wrong, he made a difference between those who lived in his region for centuries and the other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If it was the reference to the Western Herzegovina specifically. Or I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can try to clarify, Mr. President, or I'll put it to Mr. Hadzic. The video that we just saw, P58, it doesn't refer to Herzegovina Croats. Here, he is referring to Croats with blood on their hands and are wallowing in it and they will surely be held responsible for what they did. Now he says -- Mr. Hadzic has just testified that, if I may put it this way -- well, the Chamber has heard what he has to say. I'm drawing a connection between these sorts of words made here and what the Prosecution views as similar incendiary-type language in the public statements made before, that we discussed about before, involving his condemnation and singling out of Herzegovina Croats. So this is another example of Hadzic, of Mr. Hadzic inciting and stoking violence against Croats, again, in his capacity as president of the government of the SBWS. Now, in this video, he is saying that: "All Croats who stay in our region, all Croats living here for years, will be able to stay with us in the Serb region." Now, this is arguably, this is consistent with what he was saying before, the statements about the Herzegovina Croats. The Chamber may recall the earlier testimony about the distinction between those who had always lived in the region, the more peaceful ones from the flatlands, versus the more aggressive ones from the mountainous regions, such as Dalmacija and Western Herzegovina. So there is a consistency here, but it is all about stoking violence and inciting violence against Croats. That's our point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood, Mr. Hadzic spoke about the people who had blood on their hands and about Ustasha nests, et cetera, et cetera. He didn't mention any -- anyone from some particular regions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The discussion is on the record now. Would you like to have your client further questions -- questioned about this, Mr. Zivanovic, or can we move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can move on, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. President, that we need to go into private session for the next exhibit, which is tab 1578 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we have tab 760, please. 65 ter 1939.21.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Isn't that true, Mr. Hadzic, that in July of 1991, the very period we've been talking about here, you appointed Mr. Jovo Ostojic to be the commander of the Volunteer Recruitment Centre at Prigrevica? This document comes from Mr. Petrovic's book.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. And I think that no one consulted me about this, if he had been appointed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, this is the same time that you were making the appointments of the others, Mr. Malakovic, Mr. Kojic. And, here, what we see is that you're also appointing Mr. Ostojic of the Volunteer Recruitment Centre in Prigrevica. You don't recall that at all?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I remember Janko Malakovic and Ilija Kojic. I don't remember that this existed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so it's your evidence that you absolutely deny having appointed Mr. Ostojic to be the commander of this training centre?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is the first time I hear of this. I don't know whether this happened -- I mean, this is the first time I hear of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, if you could just take a moment to think back, I'll ask you one last time: Did you appoint Mr. Ostojic to be the commander of this Prigrevica training centre?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not remember that, and I don't remember that this centre existed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we take from that that you actually deny having made this appointment, you reject this document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did not do that, and I don't remember this at all, that something functioned in that sense. Had that happened, I would have remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's go to tab 421 then, which is P143. This is from a publication called "Velika Srbija." "Velika Srbija" meaning great or Greater Serbia, is that -- is my understanding of that correct, Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, but Velika Srbija could mean -- could be translated either like great Serbia or Greater Serbia, not both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, that's why I asked Mr. Hadzic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Why shouldn't we have waited for Mr. Hadzic's response, Mr. Zivanovic? I mean, if you object to Mr. Hadzic performing translation, then we could have asked the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it is just an issue of translation. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, just perhaps for -- to clarify it, I'll just read the words and perhaps the interpreters could -- could give it to us back in English. Velika Srbija.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's either great Serb or Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in paragraph 1, Mr. Hadzic, of this publication, it's referring -- this document refers to the things done by this Kragujevac Chetnik detachment. And again we see: "It was sent on its first assignment to the command of the Serbian Chetnik movement on 19 July, 1991. The detachment was to be stationed in the village of Prigrevica with other volunteers from Serbia and undergo supplementary training there." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, in fact, there was a training centre in Prigrevica where volunteers, such as members of the Chetnik Movement, came and trained and were staged before moving into Slavonia. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that information. From the information I had at the time, all volunteers who came in arrived through the barracks called Bubanj Potok in Belgrade. That's what I knew at the time. I don't know about this. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1591, 65 ter 6518.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We're going to go back in time just a little bit, Mr. Hadzic. This is a poster for a peaceful resolution -- I should say, a poster regarding -- to organise a rally for the peaceful resolution of the crisis. This is Jagodnjak on the 21st of April, and it's announcing various persons who will speak. This is the Jagodnjak rally that we've seen the film of at various times in the trial, isn't it, and which Mr. Paroski made the statements about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And here, Mr. Seselj, we know from the video that he did speak. We know that Milan Paroski did speak. Can he saw that on the video-clip. You're listed as one of the speakers. Did you speak at this event?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't even there. I see this poster for the first time now and my name on it. I wasn't invited, and, if I had been, I wouldn't have gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And Jovo Ostojic is also indicated as one of the speakers here, as president of the Regional SDS Board for Backa. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, but I cannot give evidence about that. I only know as much as the rest of you. I don't know any more. I wasn't present there, and nobody told me anything, in particular, about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But you do know that he played a role in the SDS, Serbian Democratic Party, at least as of this time. You already told us that subsequently he moved over to the Serbian Radical Party. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see now that he was in the Serbian Democratic Party, but he did not emphasise his party membership. So, at that time, I didn't even know it. But the board for Baranja was a separate board in parallel with the Vukovar board, so they organised their rallies autonomously without consulting anyone from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know when he switched and became a member of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no clue. I never discussed Jovo Ostojic with anyone. Never exchanged three words about Jovo Ostojic with anyone. Didn't know anything about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just looking at some of the names on this document, Mr. Hadzic, based on what we've seen and discussed, can we agree that Mr. Seselj, Paroski, and Jovic were all personally involved in recruiting volunteers who would come to fight in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said Seselj, Paroski, and Jovic? Those three names; right? From what I know, they did organise volunteers. But that's information I received subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tender this, 65 ter 6518.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3225, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just to stay briefly for another minute or two with Mr. Ostojic before the break, could we please have tab 1056, P3137.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that would be 65 ter 4921.8 for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] ... battle-field in Krajina. We visited today another unit of volunteers that is protecting the borders with Krajina, that during the last two years of war have been present at every place where the Serbdom and the Orthodox faith have been threatened. "One of the reasons of our visit was a successful operation carried out several days ago in which 16 Ustashas were liquidated. On this occasion, Serbian volunteers were visited by the commander of the Main Staff of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, General Mile Novakovic, and Minister Milan Martic. General Novakovic congratulated the soldiers on the successful operation and stressed that their unit can be a role model for all those who are defending Serbdom. "Novakovic: Main Staff of the Serbian army especially appreciates Serbian volunteers who came to these western parts of the Serbian state to defend it, to try to defend and defend successfully these people and these territories of ours. We appreciate you because we know that you did not come here to fight because of some personal image of yourself but because of some war glory of yours because of some egocentric interests. We know that you came to fight for freedom and the honour of Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We had no sound at all so we don't know exactly where to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- apologies for that. That's good for now and then we'll continue, and we can even go back and replay it if it would assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, just looking at the image in front of us, are you able to recognise either of the two people on the left of the screen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First one was the General Mile Novakovic. And the one with the beard is Jovo Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just for the record, tell us who was General Mile Novakovic? What was his background and what was his function at this time.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an ex-colonel of the Yugoslav People's Army, hailing from a village called Kirin in the region of Kordun, and he was the commander of the Serbian Army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You said he was an ex-colonel of the Yugoslav People's Army. In fact, during the time that he was commander of the RSK army, he was still on the payroll of the JNA, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was. They talked about it, but I'm not sure. And I tried to tell you more about him naming the village where he came from, et cetera, because that's how I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think the answer of Mr. Hadzic is not correctly transcribed. If he could repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat your last answer, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood when the Prosecutor asked who he was and where he hailed from, I gave a broader answer, saying where he was born and that he was an ex-colonel of the Yugoslav People's Army. I wasn't talking about the position he was occupying when he was photographed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, for the clarification, it would be useful to -- to read both the question and his answer between lines 19 and 24. It could be done by the Prosecution or by me or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can try to clarify it, Mr. President, although it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is actually the second sentence in the response of Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What do you take as the second -- sorry. The second sentence is which one? They talked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] They talked about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But I'm not sure. And did he say something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he said they didn't talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Hadzic. Did they talk about it or didn't they talk about it? About -- about the fact --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said we didn't discuss it. I didn't ask him who was paying his salary. We didn't ask any personal questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Time for the break. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, we were told that you have a question for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A short technical matter. When will I have the right to see my lawyers? At the end, when the Prosecutor finishes? Or at the end of the redirect? I don't know at which stage we are. I don't know who the first witness will be. I have no information whatsoever these days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, Mr. Zivanovic, I -- I thought that the directions we gave were clear enough to let you know that you can have -- you, Mr. Hadzic, can have contact with Defence counsel for the preparation of other witnesses. As from now, there is no ban on that kind of contact. So if it is not -- it is not about the substance of your testimony -- of your own testimony, there's no problem at all. Is this helpful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. But when will I have no normal contact with my Defence counsel? Do I have to wait until the end of the re-direct or when the Prosecutor finishes? Because I'm not a lawyer, all these things are not so clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That is when you step down from the witness-stand, Mr. Hadzic, and that would be after re-direct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You're welcome. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, just before the break, we were looking at the video and talking about the video that showed General Novakovic and Mr. Ostojic, and let's just play another part of that and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I believe the interpreters should still have it handy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Which one was it could you remind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That was P3137 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The Serbian volunteers who arrived in these western parts of the Serbian land to defend these people and our territories. We appreciate you because we know that you did not come here to fight because of some personal image of yours, because of some war glory, because of some egotistic interests of yours. We know that you came here to fight for the freedom and honour of the Serbian people. "Reporter: Vojvoda duke Jovo Ostojic, who is at the head of this elite unit, appealed to all the Serbs who have not yet done so to join in the ranks of the defence, because Serbdom is defended in neither Belgrade nor Knin. It is defended everywhere where Serbs are attacked. Amongst Serbian volunteers there are members of all political parties but none of them are at this moment interested in politics. They're all fighting under the single command of the Main Staff of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. "Ostojic: The motto of our soldiers is patriotism and freedom of the Serbian people and there is nothing else. We wish to defend Serbian lands. We want to defend Serbian children and Serbian mothers and to deal with the Ustasha devils in a soldierly and heroic manner. And I would send them the following message: Let them not touch young children. Let them be man enough and let them stand in the battle-field. Let them choose their own weapon. We are ready. It is very difficult for us, for me. Here there are Croatian women and children and not a hair on their heads must be touched while they thrust knives into our children and cut their throats."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, just to round this off, you were aware, since you were president of the republic, that Mr. Ostojic led a group of Chetniks, volunteers out and fought as part of the RSK armed forces then. You are aware of that; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many volunteers. I don't specifically remember that. Nobody reported that to me, in particular. I know that when Maslenica was attacked, hundreds and thousands of men came to defend that part of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I take it then that if I were to suggest to you that, as it's indicated here, he's leading a group of volunteers fighting in RSK, you would not dispute that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not disputing that. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 685, P2685.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this has already been referred to by you, I belive, already, Mr. Hadzic, and it's already in evidence this document, which is to tie this off. This is 13th of May, 1993, central homeland administration of the Serbian Chetnik movement, and if you go to the bottom of the document you see that it appears over the name of Mr. Vojislav Seselj. These are appointments, and if we go to page 5, item 13, beginning of the bottom of this page and then we'll continue to the next page. According to this, then -- and this is Dr. Seselj appointing Mr. Jovo Ostojic to be a Serbian Chetnik Vojvoda. That is a duke; correct? You knew about this at some point.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm giving you second- or third-hand evidence. I just heard about it. I believe it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then it says here. And it may be necessary to move to the next page that he -- actually, may be necessary to move to the next page of yours in B/C/S. I think we're okay in English. But it says that he organised and prepared Chetnik volunteer units across Backa and then personally led them in the war-effected territories or Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. You do know that that was, in fact, what was taking place at the time during the conflict in 1991, don't you? He was among those of the Chetnik movement fighting in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that he was in Palaca village, I think, close to Osijek, in co-ordination with the JNA, that is to say, as part of the Yugoslav People's Army, and he had with him a number of his friends from Prigrevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you knew that he came from Prigrevica with others?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about -- from Milan Milanovic, Mrgud.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know what units of the JNA Mr. Ostojic fought with in this Osijek region?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's territory of the former Osijek municipality. He was defending the Serbian village of Palaca. It was some units which was part of the Osijek brigade, I believe, but it was totally under the command of the JNA, integrated into the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So this would eventually be JNA forces that were under the command of General Biorcevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was at the beginning or at the end, but it was in that sector where Commander Biorcevic was. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So it would have been Bratic or Biorcevic, depending on the time-frame?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the proviso that Biorcevic was Chief of Staff to Bratic so the two were there at the same time. But I didn't know it at the time. I learned it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right. And then we talked about this earlier in your cross. I can't recall the date offhand, but then I believe it was in October General Bratic was killed, and at that point General Biorcevic replaced him. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'd like now to go back to the video P0058, which we looked at at the beginning of this section just to follow up on one last thing before we move on. And we're actually going to -- if we make take a moment to try to skip forward because I don't think we need to replay the whole thing again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please have the 65 ter number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: 4873.2. Let's just start it from the beginning and let it run and then we can stop.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Well, the situation is much clearer from a military point of view.
